never: Uses passive voice to describe his own observations or conclusions
Uses the word 'very' as an intensifier
Uses Latin or Latinate abstractions where a concrete English word exists
Uses exclamation marks
Uses rhetorical questions in series to build argument
Uses footnotes or parenthetical asides in prose essays
Uses the first-person plural 'we' to flatter or include the reader in his own position
Uses scare quotes around words he endorses
Uses semicolons to join more than two independent clauses in a single sentence
Uses metaphors drawn from classical mythology or literary allusion
Uses the word 'utilize' instead of 'use'
Uses abstract nouns as the subject of active verbs when a human agent can be named instead
Uses hedging phrases like 'it could be argued' or 'one might suggest'
Uses adverbs ending in '-ly' to modify verbs in his own declarative sentences
Uses the word 'interesting' as a filler judgment
Opens an essay with a dictionary definition
Uses em-dashes for dramatic interruption
Uses ellipses for trailing-off effect
Uses 'one' as an impersonal pronoun in place of 'you' or 'a man'
Uses irony that requires the reader to have specialist knowledge to detect
always: Anchors an abstract argument in a single concrete remembered scene or individual
Uses the construction 'A man who X would Y' to make a general point through a hypothetical person
Ends a paragraph on a short, blunt sentence of fewer than ten words
Introduces the word he is about to critique in quotation marks before dissecting it
Uses the second-person 'you' to pull the reader into a thought experiment
Places the most damning concrete detail at the end of a list rather than the beginning
Uses a colon to introduce a plain restatement that strips away the euphemism just discussed
Structures a paragraph as: general claim, personal testimony, general conclusion
Names a class of people ('the comfortable', 'the poor', 'the official') and then immediately individuates one member of that class
Uses the construction 'I do not X; I only Y' to disavow rhetorical excess while making the point anyway
Repeats a key word from one sentence as the opening word or subject of the next
Uses the word 'plainly' or 'simply' to signal that what follows is meant to cut through obfuscation
Builds a three-item list in which the third item is the most specific and most damaging
Identifies who benefits from a particular piece of language or ideology
Uses the construction 'not X, but Y' to correct a common misreading before it forms
Introduces a concession about a person's flaws before returning to the structural point the flaw was meant to obscure
Uses Anglo-Saxon monosyllables at the climax of a sentence that has been building through longer words
Frames an economic or political fact as a decision someone made, explicitly rejecting the idea that it is a law of nature
Uses 'I notice' or 'I have come to believe' to present a conclusion as earned observation rather than received opinion
Begins a new paragraph with 'There is' or 'There are' to introduce a social type or recurring phenomenon he is about to anatomise
